records.title: Preschool Availability in New Hampshire Public Schools
records.abstract: In spring 2024, researchers at the University of New Hampshire undertook data collection to better understand the landscape of preschool offerings in New Hampshire’s public schools. School districts provide preschool using a variety of models based on local needs. All public school districts must provide access to a free appropriate public education for preschool-aged children with an identified disability under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) Part B. Children identified under IDEA Part B have an Individualized Education Program, or IEP, to support their learning. Some districts receive Title I funding to include preschool opportunities for children who are identified as “at-risk” for learning disadvantages. Still other districts offer limited access to local children via tuition-based slots or wider community access through creative use of local taxes or grant funds. This brief includes data collected from all New Hampshire public schools with state-recorded preschool or kindergarten enrollment. The goal was to determine the number of preschool slots offered within New Hampshire public schools and whether the school districts serve preschool-aged children with and without IEPs. The data show that programs extending beyond IDEA Part B exist. However, our data collection did not include details on how such programming was funded, nor on the number of children with and without IEPs in specific classrooms or programs. Thus, from this round of data collection we cannot fully identify or fully describe the reach of preschool access in New Hampshire public schools for children without an IEP specifically.

records.title: Impact of School Canteens on School Retention and Academic Performance in the Atlantic Department (Benin)
records.abstract: In Benin, obstacles to universal access to primary education persist. In rural areas, enrolment and attendance rates remain low due to several factors. Families living in poverty may not be able to afford to send their children to school; although the government has eliminated primary school fees, parents still have to buy school uniforms and supplies. There is also an opportunity cost associated with sending girls to school, rather than keeping them at home where they can help their mothers with household chores and look after their younger siblings (School canteens in Benin to improve student enrolment and retention in partnership with parents’ associations, 2008). Prior to 2016, the school feeding system was in its infancy, with canteens operated for only three months of the year. However, thanks to determined government reforms, the school canteen system has undergone a profound transformation. The implementation of a USD 79 million has not only not only increased coverage from coverage from 30% to 75% today, but also set the ambitious target ambitious goal of achieving 100% coverage by the end of 2023 [1]. The aim of this study is to assess the impact of canteens on school retention and children’s academic performance. We conducted a descriptive and analytical diagnostic survey using a questionnaire designed for parents of schoolchildren. Canteens increase and maintain the number of children in our schools, especially when the providers start their activities, in this case those traveling long distances. Almost all the parents surveyed believe that the school canteen has had an impact on their children’s motivation to attend school and class, and consequently on their performance. For example, for all parents surveyed, the school canteen has reduced the risk of children dropping out of school, especially girls (97%), although the difference with boys (95%) remains small and is not statistically significant. What’s more, since the advent of the PNASI, in the Atlantic department, the CEP pass rate in schools with canteens far exceeds that of schools without canteens. This shows that canteens play a major and positive role in the retention and success of the schoolchildren who benefit from them.

records.title: Disentangling the antecedents of higher education mergers
records.abstract: Change is rapidly transforming the higher education market in the United States. Driven by declining birth rates following the 2008 Great Recession, a looming "demographic cliff" in 2026, growing student skepticism about the value of a college education, and stagnant public funding for higher education are creating significant challenges. The market is already reacting, with closures dominating the headlines. A recent Washington Post headline, "Colleges are now closing at a pace of one a week." However, mergers are emerging as a potential alternative to closures. The Washington Post article lists five mergers announced during the 2023-24 academic year. This study addresses a gap in the existing research by concurrently analyzing operational and economic factors influencing the recent increase in higher education institution (HEI) merger transactions. Prior studies have primarily analyzed these factors in isolation. This study identifies key variables driving the recent rise in HEI mergers by employing a probit regression model with ten years of longitudinal data from IPEDS. Understanding these factors can inform strategic decision-making for HEI leaders, potentially leading to mergers that can strengthen the future of higher education and preserve student access. The study identified six factors contributing to the current wave of mergers: tuition dependency, institution size, declining enrollment, student retention, and sufficient available net assets to support operations.

records.title: The Failure of Public Higher Education Reform in North America and Western Europe: The Need for a New Beginning
records.abstract: A consistent set of criticisms of the organisation, dynamics, and failings of public higher education (HE) has been articulated since the early 1990s. Most are on target and point to a system in freefall—expensive, ineffective, and unsatisfactory for students, faculty, many staff members, and the relevant communities they serve. Despite this, the situation in HE in North America and Europe has only worsened as neoliberal management continues to intensify management by the numbers, control of student and faculty speech, administrative bloat, and increases in tuition costs. The consequent decline in public and employer support and the approaching significant decline in birth rates, and consequently in the number of college-age students in Western industrialised countries, have not moved the powerholders in these institutions to reform the institutions in fundamental ways. I argue that piecemeal public university reforms no longer hold any promise. Only a fundamental re-creation of public HE will change the situation. This re-creation must be based on open systems dynamics, transdisciplinarity, and a focus on sustainability for the stakeholders (the faculty and students, the surrounding communities, and the larger planetary ecology). The chapter closes with an examination of what such public institutions might be like.

records.title: A study of private tuition inequality: focusing on the private tuition Gini coefficient, the Hoover index and the Palma ratio
records.venue: Korean Association For Learner-Centered Curriculum And Instruction
records.abstract: Objectives This study aims to find a way to measure the degree of inequality in private education expenditures in Korea and to analyze trends in inequality. Methods We analyzed the private education expenditures survey conducted by the Ministry of Education to find an index that indicates the inequality of private education expenditures, and obtained each index by year to under-stand the trend. Results The average private education expenditures per person is increasing, and the analysis of private education expenditures inequality using the Gini coefficient, the Hoover index, and the Palma ratio shows that inequality is increasing, especially in elementary schools. In 2020, during the COVID-19 situation, the private education Gini coefficient increased rapidly as the private education participation rate decreased in elementary and middle schools, but this phenomenon was not found in high schools. Conclusions The Gini coefficient, Hoover index, and Palma ratio, which indicate the degree of inequality in private education, can be obtained for the entire population and participants, but considering that the case where private education expenditures are 0 has a significant impact, it may be more appropriate to limit it to participants. The Gini coefficient, which indicates income inequality, is on the decline, but the Gini coefficient for private education expenditures for participants is increasing, and since private education is linked to the problems of low birth rate and local extinction that our society faces, special measures are needed to reduce private education.

records.title: Child Penalties, Child Outcomes, and Family Culture

Consumption smoothing, the cost of children, and family size desired in poor households: empirical evidence from family planning villages in Sintang Regency, the Province of West Kalimantan, Indonesia
records.abstract: There are many factors that may prevent individuals from achieving consumption smoothing, especially for poor individuals or households. Liquidity barriers for the poor can be overcome by pension programs financed by the government and intergenerational transfers. This research aims at investigating determinants of the family size decisions in poor households. This research uses primary data from survey questionnaires conducted among 447 poor households selected in Family Planning Villages throughout Sintang Regency. The family size decision is only affected by parents’ expectation of an intergenerational transfer. This variable has a significant positive effect, and the possibility of an old-age pension scheme provided by the government does not significantly affect the family size decision. This may be due to the fact that there has been no pension scheme for poor households in Indonesia. The cost of children does not influence the poor household’s family size decision. This is probably due to family package assistance provided by the government which can help reduce the cost of children. The cost of daily living, health and education costs have a significant positive effect on the burden of these costs. The findings of this study indicate that the family assistance package provided by the government does not encourage poor households to have a larger family, meaning that the provision of family assistance packages does not contradict the Family Planning Program. It also provides evidence that the government’s pension scheme for poor households can be also considered as a means of controlling the population growth, because this scheme will lower the expectation of poor households to receive intergenerational transfers.

records.title: Financial Barriers to Oncofertility Services for Adolescent & Young Adults
records.abstract: Oncofertility Services: Oncofertility ServicesCancer and its treatments can lead to short- and long-term side effects that can affect a patient's quality of life both during and after treatment. Hair loss, nausea, weight loss, pain, and irritation at the treatment site are all side effects of systemic therapies. Loss of an organ or limb, permanent disabilities, and death are all potential outcomes of cancer. Of course, there also are social burdens: strains on familial relationships, friendships, and romantic partners; unemployment; and financial hardships. For adolescents and young adults (AYA) with cancer, however, there seems to be one burden that specifically and uniquely affects this vulnerable group—the threat of infertility and difficulty accessing fertility preservation services due to financial hardships and lack of insurance coverage. In a recent study conducted by the University of Michigan's Adolescent and Young Adult Oncology Program (AYA CaRES) in partnership with Rogel Cancer Center and C.S. Mott Children's Hospital's AYA Clinical Oncology Program, 27 AYA cancer patients whose cancer and/or treatment increased their risk of infertility participated in 60-minute interviews to discuss their cancer journeys, future goals, and experiences with fertility preservation (J Adolesc Young Adult Oncol 2023; https://doi.org/10.1089/jayao.2022.0055). It's important to note that the National Cancer Institute defines AYA as a patient between the ages of 15 and 39. However, in different clinical settings, AYAs may be considered as young as 12 and up to 45 years old. In this study, the participating patients were between the ages of 12 and 25 years old. “One of our questions in the interview helped us talk to young people about what they think about their futures: Does being a parent factor into your vision of yourself in the future?” said Nina Francis-Levin, PhD, MSW, a postdoctoral fellow in the University of Michigan Department of Internal Medicine's Division of Metabolism, Endocrinology, and Diabetes. “I asked [a 12-year-old cancer patient]: ‘What are your dreams for your future?’ She, unprompted, said: ‘I wanted to be a mom, but now I can't.’ That really stuck with me.” Studying Fertility Journeys In an interview with Oncology Times, Francis-Levin explained the financial consequences of cancer on AYA patients and how these consequences affect their access to fertility preservation. Factors such as high treatment costs, disease impact on education and vocational training, and difficulty in accessing health insurance coverage can increase cancer care costs. Francis-Levin noted that a lack of health insurance is common for this group because they are often inconsistently employed in jobs that provide coverage. Also, some patients, particularly those around 26 years old, are aging out of their parents' coverage. While dealing with a lack or loss of insurance coverage, other social determinants unique to this age group—entry-level salaries and tuition or student loan debt—make the high costs of health care even more unaffordable. Although the financial impact of cancer treatment is a well-known burden on AYA patients, little was known of its impact on AYA access to fertility preservation and assisted reproductive technology (ART) until recently. “Something different is going on with this group compared to younger kids or older adults, and some of those things are going to college, starting a career, romantic relationships, building a family, moving out of home, and becoming financially independent,” Francis-Levin said. “There are so many milestones to strive toward to gain independence, agency, and independent personhood that can be compromised, delayed, or rerouted when cancer comes into the picture. There are things that get disorganized and one of the main major concerns for this group is fertility because becoming infertile as a young adult or teenager can be very devastating, especially if somebody wants to have children in the future or may not know if they want to have children.” According to Francis-Levin, approximately 80 percent of AYA patients may experience fertility impairment, whether that's temporary or permanent, and this can be caused by solid tumors affecting the reproductive system, surgeries to remove affected parts of the reproductive system, treatments that affect hormone levels, and chemotherapies or radiation therapies that may damage the reproductive organs. Yet, fertility preservation and ART are inconsistently covered across health care insurance plans, and fertility treatments can account for some of the highest out-of-pocket expenses for AYA patients and their families. A Look at the Costs A recent retrospective study published in Psycho-Oncology found that, for patients assigned male at birth, fertility preservation (e.g., sperm banking, testicular sperm extraction, and electroejaculation) can cost between $1,000 and $12,000 in out-of-pocket expenses, while options for patients with female reproductive organs (e.g., egg, embryo, and ovarian tissue freezing) can fall within the $10,000-$15,000 range before annual storage fees (2018; https://doi.org/10.1002/pon.4898). Additional ART options—IVF (single cycle, $12,400; treatment per live birth; $40,000-$60,000), gestational carrier or surrogate ($100,000-$150,000), and domestic adoptions ($30,000-$40,000)—can drive up medical costs and debt. Leuprolide, an injectable medication that protects the ovarian reserve, is one of the more affordable options for patients because it is more likely to be covered by insurance plans. “Even if somebody may not necessarily be infertile right after their treatment, we still have concerns about bodily changes and hormonal changes that make conceiving more difficult, more uncomfortable, and more uncertain,” Francis-Levin said. “I just want to stress that part of the reason [fertility preservation] is very hard to research and counsel among other reasons—including the fact that it is so expensive—is that it is so individualized and the future of somebody's fertility or family-making goals may not necessarily be known. We may know that a patient is fertility impaired, but we don't know for sure if it will come back or not, or how one's feelings about parenthood may change after cancer.” Of the 27 survey participants, 17 patients utilized a variety of fertility preservation/ART, but where the money came from to pay for those services was the main point of interest for the University of Michigan team. Several prominent themes emerged from the patients' interviews: varied access to health insurance, presence of parental/guardian support, reliance upon financial aid, negotiating infertility risk, and lack of preparation for long-term costs. Many participants reported reliance on their parents for health care coverage because they did not have their own. This resulted in some patients not knowing whether fertility preservation was covered. Others discussed that their insurance covered some, but not all, fertility preservation, while others, unfortunately, had no coverage at all. Notably, a 23-year-old patient critiqued the health care system due to the lack of universal coverage for oncofertility services. For expenses not covered by insurance, many patients turned to their families for financial support. Others even claimed that fertility preservation would not be possible without parental/guardian support. However, the patients who reported financial support from their familial unit also expressed mixed feelings of guilt and gratitude, and some felt their support network hid the costs of fertility preservation to relieve any undue burdens of guilt. Similarly to patients who reported a total lack of insurance coverage, a handful of patients, including one 12-year-old patient, reported that their family could not afford out-of-pocket costs for fertility treatments. Unfortunately, this was the deciding factor for these disadvantaged patients and their future parenthood. “I wasn't going be able to afford it and I didn't have anyone to help me,” a 21-year-old patient reported to Francis-Levin. “So, I just let it go.” Several patients noted financial aid resources made it possible to utilize fertility preservation/ART. For some of the patients, this was a deciding factor in pursuing these options. “I figured [with financial support] I might as well.” Some of these resources included support programs (e.g., Livestrong, Expect Miracles Foundation) that patients discovered through their health care providers, partnering with crowdfunding platforms like GoFundMe, and strategizing with aid organizations, such as Worth the Wait, to store gametes in states with lower storage fees. More male than female patients reported negotiating infertility risk by weighing their risk against the cost of fertility preservation. For some patients, minimal risk of infertility merited fertility preservation regardless of cost. Others strategized to maximize their fertility preservation investment. For example, a 24-year-old patient reported that he banked sperm twice because the storage cost was a flat rate and one more session was only a slight increase in cost. For some patients who felt agnostic toward having children of their own, the cost did not factor into their choice to not pursue fertility preservation. On the other hand, female patients were more likely to discuss concerns about long-term costs and future planning. Although, many patients were unaware of future steps in fertility preservation and associated expenses with oncofertility treatment, like storing gametes and using ART (such as IVF) to become pregnant. “This is not easy for anyone, but this is especially not easy for someone who is young and going through cancer,” Francis-Levin said. “This is a group that needs support and we don't know a lot about what young people need. We know some things, but we need to know more about how we can create and develop long-term, supportive services to help people over the course of their life with their family-building goals in the context of impaired fertility both during and after cancer.” Currently, 17 states offer oncofertility coverage for patients whose cancer or cancer treatments threaten infertility. The work of researchers like Francis-Levin and her colleagues at the University of Michigan—namely Brad Zebrack, PhD, Molly Moravek, MD, Anao Zhang, PhD, Emily Walling, MD, and Rashmi Chugh, MD—shine a light on this unique issue that largely affects AYA cancer patients. However, legislative action is required to bring about widespread change for this vulnerable population and organizations like the Alliance for Fertility Preservation, the Oncofertility Consortium, The Breasties, and FORCE have done great work in advocating for the reproductive rights of AYA patients. Elizabeth Galamba is a contributing writer.

records.title: The Korean Residency Crisis: A Cautionary Tale for U.S. Health Care
records.abstract: residents, income, strike, reimbursement: Asan Medical Center, the largest hospital in South Korea, was nearly empty after residents, medical students, and attendings went on strike.FigureThe vast majority of South Korean residents and medical students went on strike, throwing the entire health care system of a wealthy industrialized nation into chaos early this year. Tertiary care centers that act as teaching hospitals lost up to 40 percent of their working physicians overnight. Like residents training worldwide, South Korean residents receive low wages and often work 80 to 100 hours per week. (J Grad Med Educ. 2024;16[4]:402; https://tinyurl.com/298ntxfv.) Countless procedures were canceled, and access to care was increasingly difficult. It is hard, if not impossible, for U.S. residents and medical students to imagine leaving positions they worked so hard to attain. But U.S. residents have been pushing back over the past few years against wages that cannot fully support residency training in cities with a high cost of living and benefits packages that do not support wellness and growing families. Twenty-eight U.S. training hospitals had increased wages and benefits through negotiation with resident unions as of August. (Substack. Emergency Medicine Workforce Newsletter. Aug. 26, 2024; https://tinyurl.com/286w2ns8.) But that is a fraction of the total number of residents in training programs; what would happen if 90 percent of U.S. residents walked off the job as South Korean residents did in February? Challenges in South Korea South Korea is a remarkable country. Ravaged by occupation and war, it rose from the ashes in the 1950s to become an industrialized economic powerhouse. Surrounded by water on three sides and a hostile neighbor to the north, it is effectively an island the size of Oregon (PBS. https://tinyurl.com/394k6dm7) with more than 51 million people, about the same as California and Pennsylvania combined. (World Population Review. 2024; https://tinyurl.com/vbj9yy9r.) Manufacturing giants Samsung, Kia, and Hyundai call South Korea home. It is a profoundly patriarchal society, however, with women earning 30 percent less than men, the widest gender pay gap in the industrialized world. (Washington Post. Feb. 21, 2024; https://tinyurl.com/mvp5as74.) The birth rate is also falling, as it is in many wealthy nations. South Korea's fertility rate is one of the lowest in the world, at 1.1 births per woman. (Macrotrends. https://tinyurl.com/y8kzs4wn.) I visited the capital, Seoul, before the pandemic, and was impressed by the country's efficiency, beauty, culture, and wealth. The National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) is a single-payer system that covers almost all South Korean citizens and attempts to control costs that often result in lower physician reimbursement. Medical school is combined with undergraduate studies, resulting in six years of study before residency training. Like the United States, acceptance to one of South Korea's 40 medical schools is highly competitive. Unlike the United States, tuition is only around $8000 per year. The average physician's salary in South Korea is around $220,000, more than five times the median income. (The Korea Herald. May 15, 2024.) Physicians are not only subject to malpractice litigation, but they can also face criminal charges that result in long, multiyear trials. Attacking the Residents What tipped the scales that caused so many of the brightest young adults in South Korea to walk away from a future job with prestige and a dependable high income? The answer is a little odd. The government wanted to add more medical students. The NHIS, which controls the number of medical student positions, raised the annual quota by 2000 from the previous cap of 3058, a 65 percent increase. (J Grad Med Educ. 2024;16[4]:402; https://tinyurl.com/298ntxfv.) This makes complete sense on one level. Like wealthy nations with an aging population, South Korea needs more physicians, particularly in rural locations. (J Grad Med Educ. 2024;16[4]:402; https://tinyurl.com/298ntxfv.) Shortly after the government's announcement, however, residents and medical students walked off the job, and 12,000 attending physicians followed them over the next few months in a show of solidarity. (Channel News Asia. https://tinyurl.com/3bmfdzwy.) What are these striking health care workers trying to achieve? The answer: money. NHIS funds health care through a combination of insurance premiums and government taxes. This does not cover the total cost of health care for their rapidly aging population, however, which averages more doctor visits per person than any other country. (Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. 2021; https://tinyurl.com/mu7va746.) The government's solution was to increase the number of medical students dramatically while aggressively controlling costs through lower reimbursement. The residents and medical students saw this plan as a direct threat to their future income and cohesively moved to force the government to reconsider. Their position is that a large increase in physicians in a market with tight spending controls will negatively affect their futures. The strikers are attempting to nip the government's “solution” in the bud before it becomes their dystopic reality. The government fought back by aggressively attacking the strikers in the media as greedy and ordered striking residents back to work. The residents, however, remain on strike. (Channel News Asia. June 27, 2024; https://tinyurl.com/3bmfdzwy.) A Dangerous Game Interestingly, emergency medicine's recent experiences are similar to those of the South Korean residents. The emergency physician workforce study created a similar situation to NHIS's announcement of a dramatic increase in medical students. The paper's prediction of a large surplus of residency-trained emergency physicians in 2030 generated anxiety among U.S. medical students considering EM training. (Ann Emerg Med. 2021;78[6]:726; https://tinyurl.com/ysbsj9wz.) Emergency medicine derives roughly half its revenue from government programs (PLoS One. 2021;16[10]:e0258182; https://tinyurl.com/mrzayeac), and the U.S. students feared the negative impact on their future income and chose other specialties. Predictably, the subsequent matches in 2022 and 2023 were disastrous before a solid rebound last spring. Obviously, the health care system in South Korea and the United States are different, and, like all markets, health care systems must balance cost and revenue. Like South Korea's NHIS, the U.S. government and private health insurance corporations try to control the cost of health care for our aging population. This includes looking for cheaper alternatives to provide care by empowering less educated nonphysician providers and capping reimbursement for costly medications and procedures. Whether a nation uses a single-payer or multipayer health care system, South Korea's experience is a cautionary tale. It may seem easy to repair balance sheets by exploiting overworked residents with limited ability to fight back. The assumption that residents will take the hit because they are more focused on their future earnings is a dangerous game, and all health care organizations would do well to pay attention. DR. records.title: Fertility Rate under the Dual Pressure of Raising Children and the Elderly
records.venue: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
records.abstract: At present, China is in a new normal of population development characterized by low birth rates and a highly aging population, and the trend is increasingly deepening. In this context, this article first classifies the reasons for the low fertility rate through theory and then analyzes the pressure of raising children and taking care of the elderly from the perspective of people during the fertility window period. Through data and analysis, it has been found that the economic pressure on contemporary young people is particularly concentrated on the education expenditure for children and the dependency ratio for the elderly. Finally, this article proposes some practical solutions, attempting to develop the role of the elderly labor force in intergenerational education through economic policies and social support. These plans can simultaneously utilize the two demographic characteristics of China's low fertility rate and high aging population, and accelerate the improvement of the fertility support system by helping young people obtain intergenerational care.

Практика применения мер, направленных на снижение бедности, c учетом уровня нуждаемости семей в сопоставимых с Россией зарубежных странах
records.abstract: В большинстве стран существует социальная поддержка бедных, которым предоставляются социальные выплаты. Все эти программы обеспечивают адресность, но с разной степенью, в лучших случаях 1/5 беднейших по доходам достается до 4/5 всех социальных выплат. Успешность адресности, прежде всего, зависит от отбора получателей проверки нуждаемости домохозяйства и его имущественной обеспеченности. Кроме того, многие меры социальной поддержки предоставляются на основании социального контракта, то есть используют требования или условия, которые обязательны к выполнению получателями. В большинстве стран ОЭСР и стран Евросоюза адресная помощь правоустановливается с государственного (национального) уровня, и лишь в отдельных случаях полномочия по ее установлению находятся на субнациональных уровнях. В большинстве рассматриваемых статьей стран размер получаемого пособия тем больше, чем больше размер семьи и чем больше в ней иждивенцев. Большинство адресных мер используют явные или неявные шкалы для пересчета размера пособия в зависимости от состава семьи.Особенностью мер, предусматривающих подтягивание доходов получателей до некоторого минимально гарантированного уровня, является то, что такие меры, как правило, обеспечивают неполный охват целевой группы. Размер адресных выплат находится в интервале от 2до 32 от средней заработной платы на человека в случае семейной пары. Во всех этих странах, в отличие от Российской Федерации, помощь по поддержке уровня доходов оказывается с учетом имущественной обеспеченности заявителей, а отношении учета в доходах социальных выплат эти страны демонстрируют различную практику, как сходную с российской, так и отличную от нее, в частности, это касается учета пособия по безработице. Особый интерес для российской практики представляет применение таких инструментов, как минимальный неучитываемый доход (Earningsdisregards) и дифференциация размера выплаты в зависимости от уровня дохода (Benefitwithdrawalratewithregardtoearnedincome). Social support to the poor in the form of cash benefits exists in the majority of countries. All such programs provide some level of targeting, albeit to a varying extent. At best, 1/5 of the poorest individuals get 4/5 of the total amount of social support allowances. The accuracy of targeting depends primarily on the screening procedures, i.e. means testing and applying assets filters. Also, social support programs often require the conclusion of a social contract which establishes the obligations of the participants or the conditions that they should meet. In the majority of OECD and EU nations targeted assistance legislated at the national level, and only in occasional cases the authority to establish such programs rests with subnational governments. In the majority of countries considered the amount of the benefit depends on family size: the bigger the family and the more dependents it has, the larger is the benefit. Explicit or implicit equivalence scales are usually applied to adjust the amount of the benefit to the composition of the household. Income support programs that seek to bring the family income up to a certain minimal threshold usually do not provide for full coverage of the target group. The amount of targeted benefits typically falls within the range of 2to 32 of the average wage per capita (in case of a two partners household). Unlike the Russian Federation, in all the countries considered income support programs require the application of assets filters, while the policies of regard or disregard of social support benefits for the purpose of assessing total family income differ from country to country, in some cases going in line with the Russian practices, in other cases going against them, as in the case of regard or disregard of the unemployment benefit, for instance. Of special interest for Russia is the application of such instruments as earnings disregards and benefit withdrawal rate with regard to earned income.

records.title: “Explaining Variation in Child Penalties: The Role of Gender Norms and Policies”
records.abstract: This paper contributes to understanding global variation in child and marriage penalties by focusing on the role of patriarchal control, gender norms, and public policies. We introduce a new measure of gender norms, the Control Index, which captures women’s ‘freedom to choose’ in key areas of daily life, including mobility, marital choices, workplace rights, and financial independence. Using data from nearly 60 countries, we investigate the extent to which patriarchal control influences the child and marriage penalties, trying to disentangle the still unexplained part of the gender gap. Our findings reveal that higher levels of patriarchal control are strongly associated with larger marriage penalties. In particular, control over marriage decisions is closely correlated with both higher child and marriage penalties, while restrictions on women’s financial autonomy contributes mainly to explaining marriage penalties. This suggests that, in addition to childcare-support policies, financial inclusion for women, could mitigate the effects of patriarchal control and conservative gender norms. Our analysis underscores the importance of addressing these norms alongside public policy interventions to reduce gender disparities in the labour market. JEL Classification Code: J13-fertility, family planning, childcare, children, youth; J16-economics of gender, non-labor discrimination; J22-time allocation and labor supply

records.title: The family ability to pay for health care expenditures on malaria treatment in Cameroon
records.abstract: This thesis is concerned with the development of a methodology for identifying indicators of family's ability to pay for health care expenditures on malaria treatment. It also examines the possible trade-off between health care and other basic needs such as education and food amongst the common family responses to payment difficulties under the combined user fee burdens from various essental social sectors in Cameroon. The assumption underlying the analysis is that from the perspective of family as a whole, the affordability of costs for primary health care together with other basic services is pertinent to reach the goals of Health For All by year 2000. The descriptive cross-sectional family survey has bee designed for data collction. The data are used to estimate two binomial logit models. a multiomial logit model (choice of copig=n strategies : forego eduction. cut food consumption, sell productive assets, or borrow cash). and a multiple regression model for health care expenditures on malaria teatment. Since the approach is methodological. the questionnaire is developed. but the real data are not collected in the field. Hypothetical data denerated from three different multipurpose family surveys are used to test the models. The main empirical result of this study is that the family's ability to pay for malaria treatment costs is responsive to changes in income. savings, fee exemptions, insurane co-payment, productive assets ownership (e.g. land). percapita consumption, family size. number of employed members in the family, number of children under five years old. number pregnant women. preventive measures. sex of head of the family. principal source of income. and residence. This finding is comparable to other studies on the affordability of health care in developing countries. The results of this study outline some specific indicators which should be used by health staff when grating fee exemptions. It also demonstrates that policy initiatives must be appropriate to local contexts and disease patterns with more emphasis on preventive measures. Although, the methodological decisions for improving equity access to health care of the poor families can be ascertained. the conclusion argues that only where those findings are indeed robust should they be emphasized and confirmed with the real primary data collected through the proposed questionnaire at the level of families. Finally, this study has its limitations. All coping strategies are not investigated. For example, the consequences of the decision to delay or not seeking treatment. In addition. many of the issues of ability to pay require qualitative indepth investigation of amily priority-setting and expenditure patterns.

records.title: The cost of raising a child: Equivalence scales in the United States
records.abstract: As fertility rates drop to another historical low, understanding the economic burden of child-rearing on household income, a main economic reason for falling birth rate, has become more crucial than ever. This study calculates a subjective equivalence scale explaining how much the income of a two-adult, one-child household should increase to maintain the same level of life satisfaction as a two-adult household, using a nationally representative U.S. sample. The results suggest that the equivalence scale for a two-adult, one-child household is 1.18, indicating that raising a child costs 18 % of a two-adult household’s income. Our analysis indicates that programs like the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) and the National School Lunch Program (NSLP) may be overly generous for households with one child, while the tax deduction policy does not cover child-rearing costs sufficiently.

records.title: A Post-War ‘Underclass’ in Affluent North America: Black Family Instability, Human Capital Theory, and Gary Becker’s New Household Economics
records.abstract: From the 1960s onwards, New Household economists like Theodore Schultz and Gary Becker shifted focus onto the poverty-alleviating impacts of family investment in human capital. This move was informed, first, by increased cultural and political awareness of what Becker referred to as an impoverished ‘underclass’ (1964/1993); second, by the social movements, including civil rights challenges to racial discrimination in schools and labour markets; and third, by government debates during the War on Poverty about the causes of Black family instability. Becker explained family instability as a rational response to price changes in the goods – including children – that families wanted. Given a set of preferences for basic commodities, and facing a defined range of choices, families were conceptualised as maximising utility, subject to constraints of income and time. This permitted hypotheses about how wages and human capital investment affected the cost of children, with effects on family formation and dissolution, fertility, and care-provision by women. As for poverty-alleviation, Becker favoured low-interest education loans. He rejected progressive income taxation and family welfare for incentivising underinvestment in education. Compensatory education programmes would fail by being offset. These policy positions were described by Nancy Folbre and Randy Albelda as a War on the Poor.

records.title: Birthing a Nation: Political Legitimacy and Health Policy in Hastings Kamuzu Banda's Malawi, 1962–1980
records.abstract: Drawing upon archives in Malawi, the UK and the USA, this article explores the place of public-sector medicine in President Hastings Kamuzu Banda’s ideology of social protection in post-colonial Malawi. In the midst of internecine strife with his cabinet soon after independence, Banda abandoned health-care user fees, provided free food to hospital inpatients and promised new medical facilities. Later, Banda disregarded international advisers by refusing to promote contraception. Though some commentators attributed this policy to Banda’s conservatism, birth control also ran counter to his regime’s carefully constructed symbolism of abundance. Malawi’s government was not unique in opposing outside efforts at population control, but Banda’s ideology, which invoked what anthropologists of the 1970s called ‘wealth-in-people’, made mass sterilisation and intrauterine device (IUD) campaigns particularly unacceptable. Banda also made grand displays of his government’s new hospitals. While he would not devote significant domestic resources to health, he mobilised funds from external donors, particularly governments facing their own crises of legitimacy. This article, then, complicates the existing literature on health in Kamuzu Banda’s Malawi. While Banda did not consider health a priority, his reliance on symbols of abundance, health and fertility left him vulnerable to critique and compelled him to direct a modicum of resources toward public sector health facilities and to keep care at those facilities free of charge .

records.title: The Cost of Children
Revitalizing Interest among MBBS Graduates in Pursuing Anatomy as Career Option: A Timely Necessity
records.abstract: In recent decades, the field of anatomy—especially its academic and research branches—has witnessed a disturbing and persistent decline in the number of MBBS graduates opting to pursue it as a professional career.[1] This is not an issue of personal choice but an outcome of systemic ideologies and structural issues that have influenced the position of anatomy in the medical education system.[2] Anatomy remains the bedrock of medical sciences, forming the basis for both surgical procedures and radiological diagnosis, yet its significance has been increasingly overlooked. Anatomy is too frequently seen by students as a dry, preclinical subject lacking the glitz and perceived status accorded clinical specialties.[3] This trend is not limited to anatomy alone —postgraduate (PG) seats in nearly all pre-clinical and para-clinical subjects consistently go unfilled, reflecting a broader pattern of declining interest among medical graduates. Annually 600–800 PG seats remain vacant in pre- and paraclinical subjects.[4] The cause of this lack of interest is complex. The reduced direct patient contact, relatively slower professional advancement, and less instant monetary rewards that are part of preclinical specialisms have all been factors in the waning appeal of anatomy. In addition, the historical approaches to teaching, cadaveric dissection, formaldehyde exposure, rote learning, and chalk-and-board lectures, have failed to keep step with the developing digital culture of contemporary students.[5,6] This mismatch between pedagogy and student enthusiasm has also deterred prospective anatomists, resulting in fewer qualified anatomists available across the country in spite of increasing demand for faculty to teach MBBS students. From a curricular standpoint, anatomy education in many medical schools of United States has been transformed into highly integrated, system-based courses that emphasize active learning and clinically relevant content.[7,8] Similarly, biomedical science departments have largely embraced integration, often merging and rebranding to highlight their research-oriented focus. Consequently, anatomists, and the field of anatomy as a whole, may have experienced a loss of professional identity as traditional “Departments of Anatomy” were merged with other basic departments of science, many of which no longer highlight anatomy in their names.[9] If effective steps are not taken to address the shortage of anatomical science educators, the issue is likely to escalate in the coming decade. As more programs rely on anatomy instruction and student enrollments continue to grow, the demand for educators in the anatomical sciences is expected to increase accordingly. Teaching faculty have an outsized influence on the student experience at anatomy. Students get influenced by uninterested and unhelpful faculties. To further overcome this hindrance, anatomy should be taught as a fascinating subject and inspiring lectures by which undergraduate students get motivated to take up PG in anatomy. Anatomy should continue to provide engaging coursework and hands-on laboratory experiences that foster transferable skills like critical thinking.[10] One concern about pursuing a career in anatomy is the perceived lack of lucrative job opportunities. To address this, the field should provide more information on career paths and facilitate networking events, helping current students become aware of the diverse professional opportunities available.[11] It is encouraging that several medical institutes have pledged to offer tuition fee waivers, free boarding and lodging, stipends, and guaranteed employment upon course completion in order to attract postgraduate (PG) students to pre-clinical and para-clinical subjects—especially anatomy, which faces the most acute shortage.[11] Anatomy departments of various institutions must integrate clinical rotations, simulation-based learning, and interdisciplinary research opportunities and maintain optimistic postgraduate teaching. In NEET PG 2023, the Medical Counselling Committee reduced the minimum qualifying percentile, meaning that even those with zero percentile scores can be eligible for counseling. This was done to ensure that vacant medical seats are filled.[12,13] The qualifying percentile was reduced to 5th percentile for all categories in 2025. The main reason for this reduction was to prevent seats from going vacant, especially in preclinical and paraclinical branches.[14] The ongoing crisis in anatomical education—marked by severe faculty shortages and declining student engagement—demands urgent reforms from regulatory authorities like the National Medical Commission (NMC). A critical solution lies in integrating anatomists into adjunct clinical roles, such as outpatient consultations, radiological diagnostics, surgical planning, cytogenetic testing, and genetic counselling. These roles capitalise on their expertise in structural biology and clinical correlations, bridging the gap between foundational science and patient care. Anatomy transcends its traditional preclinical boundaries—it is periclinical and postclinical. Anatomists, equipped with mastery of human morphology and emerging technologies like 3D modelling, are uniquely positioned to enhance diagnostic accuracy and therapeutic outcomes. Their involvement in multidisciplinary care teams would not only elevate the discipline’s relevance but also address career stagnation by offering diverse professional pathways. To further modernise the field, statutory bodies must introduce superspecialization programs such as DM degrees in Neuroanatomical Sciences (focusing on neurodegenerative disorders), Clinical Embryology (for fertility and developmental biology), and Cytogenetics (integrating molecular diagnostics). To support passionate academics and clinician-scientists, there should be well-designed advanced residency or fellowship programs. Broadening knowledge and skills in areas like Immunohistochemistry, Clinical and Surgical Anatomy, Cross-sectional Anatomy, and Endoscopic Anatomy will not only enhance patient care and research but also help nurture a new wave of highly skilled anatomists and medical professionals.These advanced tracks would empower anatomists to lead in areas like precision medicine, reproductive health, and translational research, ultimately repositioning anatomy as a cornerstone of innovation in 21st-century healthcare. Faculty development programs, conferences, continued medical education, workshops, etc., like those encouraged by subject associations, should focus on pedagogical innovations, making the subject more engaging.[15-17] A truly enriching experience in anatomy comes from more than just textbooks—it’s about being part of a community where the faculty fosters a healthy and supportive work environment. It’s where peers encourage each other and there are exciting opportunities to collaborate with pioneers who inspire and lead the field. Having access to excellent resources like a well-curated anatomy museum, fully equipped libraries, cutting-edge virtual dissection tables, and digitized histology labs makes learning not only effective but also inspiring and enjoyable.[18] Policy-level interventions are needed to ensure parity in promotional pathways and remuneration for preclinical faculty. Hence, we urge attempts should be made from all levels to enable surge in MBBS graduates to opt for anatomy as a specialty and bridge the existing gap between demand and supply.

records.title: Career, Family, and IVF: The Impact of Involuntary Childlessness and Fertility Treatment
Fertility and Promotions:Academic Careers of Economists over 40 Years in Denmark
records.abstract: The arrival of children often takes place early in the research career. For many researchers, the life-changing and demanding event of becoming a parent overlap with the period the researcher has to show high levels of research productivity with the aim of gaining tenure, or an equivalent promotion to a professorship. It is important to understand how having children contributes to the 'the leaky pipeline' of women and which factors mitigate or exacerbate gender gaps in attrition following parenthood. Our project asks how fertility decisions, and specifically their timing, can affect women's academic careers in Economics. We will study this question with administrative data from Denmark covering the uni-linked with high-quality bibliometric data from Scopus. To understand how the arrival of children affects productivity and how this maps on women's probability to successful career in academia, we first estimate the unconditional child penalty of women and men economists on career progression (i.e. attrition and promotion). We then move on to estimate the child penalty of women and men economists on productivity outcomes, namely number of publications and quality of publications. While being aware that productivity is endogenous to fertility, we will estimate whether the child penalty in career progression persists once family outcomes will allow us to compare whether the child penalty caries across insights into how the timing of children interacts with the pressure on early career productivity and what extent this disadvantages women. Finally, we will explore under which circumstances gender gaps are mitigates and focus on two channels: first, the current position held by the researcher and the structure of promotion and characteristics of their workplace and second, the individual circumstances depending on their partners' career path.

records.title: Fertility in Sub-Saharan Africa: The Interplay between Policy, Culture, and Intra-Household Bargaining
Forgive Us Our Debts, as We Forgive Our Debtors
records.abstract: Richard Vedder believes that the crisis in American higher education and other contemporary social problems can be traced directly to the explosive growth of federal student loans since the mid-twentieth century. These problems include unaffordable tuition, expanding university bureaucracies, lower academic standards, housing affordability, and declining marriage and birth rates. What, if anything, Vedder asks, should be done?

records.title: The impact of terminating universal primary education on fertility: Evidence from Kenya
records.abstract: This paper investigates the educational impact on fertility caused by the termination of universal primary education (UPE) in Kenya. Although previous studies have used the introduction of UPE as a natural experiment, we focus on a unique policy change, namely, the termination of UPE. By using six waves of the Kenya Demographic and Health Survey (KDHS), our paper presents the statistically significant discontinuity in female years of education at the termination of UPE. The termination of UPE led to a decrease of 0.57 years in of female education. Using a fuzzy regression discontinuity design, we identify the impacts of education on both onset of fertility and total fertility. One additional year of female education delays onset of fertility by 0.67 years and reduces total fertility by 0.21 fewer children by the age of 46 years. As for the mechanism of these changes, we explore three possible pathways: labor participation, knowledge of contraception, and assortative mating.

records.title: Household factors influencing child dropout in government-aided primary schools; case study: Wakiso district
records.abstract: The study examined the household factors influencing child dropout in government aided primary schools in Wakiso district. Universal primary education has registered tremendous enrolment figures in the past years but there is still evidence showing that not all children are able to complete the seven-year primary education cycle as there significant dropouts. Therefore, the study sought to investigate child dropout in primary schools in the context of household factors such as parental education, child gender, number of school going age children, the household head health status and employment status. The major objective of the study was to examine the factors influencing child drop out in government aided primary schools with specific reference to house-related factors. The specific objectives include; to establish the relationship between parents’ level of education and child dropout from school, to examine the relationship between child’s gender and child dropout from school, to establish the relationship between number of primary school going age children in the household and child dropout in school, to assess whether health status of household members has an influence on child dropout from the school and to establish the relationship between household head employment status and child dropout from the school. This study used primary data primary collected from the field survey and secondary data was also gathered through literature review from various publications, journals and internet. The study used a cross-sectional design that involved collecting data on various issues related to household factors influencing child drop out in government aided schools at a single period in time. Univariate Analysis capturing descriptive statistics such as frequencies, percentages and cumulative frequencies were used to describe participants’ responses on the variables under consideration. Bivariate analysis using the chi square statistic was used to investigate whether distributions of categorical variables differ from one another. A multivariate analysis using a binary logistic regression model was run to establish the relationships between the independent variables and dependent variable. Findings from the study showed that the child gender preferred, with a base of female was statistically significant given that the p-value of 0.002 and the odds ratio 0.432 .This meant that male children had less chances of dropping out of school than their female counterparts. A positive significant relationship between the number of school going age children in the house hold and child drop was established with a p value 0.003 with the odds ratio of 0.614. This implied that an increase in the number of children in the household from 3 to 4 would significantly lead to child drop out form school. The study recommended government to promote girl- child education, encourage manageable family sizes, improve health services, focus on creating employment opportunities and enhance household incomes to reduce poverty levels.

records.title: Germany and International Student Mobility
records.abstract: Abstract Germany plays an influential role in global and European international student mobility (ISM). This is evidenced by its active involvement in initiatives such as the ERASMUS program, the Bologna Process, and the establishment of the European Higher Education Area (EHEA). As a popular destination for international students from populous countries such as India, China, and Russia, and for forcibly displaced students seeking refuge, such as those from Ukraine following the war initiated by Russia in 2022, Germany maintains an open attitude toward ISM. This can be explained by demographic factors, such as an aging population, a declining birth rate, and a decentralized egalitarian higher education system, where the housing market and competition with local students for educational resources and study choices have relatively little impact. Traditionally, German students prioritize proximity over university hierarchy and reputation and tend to study at nearby universities. Faced with an aging population and declining numbers of local students at regional universities, public universities in the regions often resort to recruiting international students in order to secure state financial support, which also applies to international students, and to maintain the attractiveness of the universities and regional cities through internationalization and academic exchanges. However, challenges remain regarding the accountability of public funding for ISM activities, given the absence of tuition fees for both domestic and international students. The tuition-free model of ISM also has implications for international student support services, such as post-study employment assistance. Although there have been continuous efforts to integrate international students into German society, language and cultural barriers still pose significant challenges, particularly for students and graduates of English-taught study programs. To address these challenges, the improvement of ISM data collection to support evidence-based policymaking and international cooperation in higher education is taken seriously in Germany by key stakeholders, such as DAAD (German: Deutscher Akademischer Austauschdienst/English: German Academic Exchange Service) and DZHW (German: Deutsches Zentrum für Hochschul- und Wissenschaftsforschung/English: German Centre for Higher Education Research and Science Studies). Since 2001, they have jointly produced the series Wissenschaft weltoffen, which provides comprehensive and detailed facts and figures on the internationality of studies and research in Germany and worldwide on an annual basis. Meanwhile, Germany remains committed to shaping ISM and the development of the EHEA, prioritizing global stability, diplomatic relations, and the needs of the labor market over commodification and commercialization of international education services.

EFFECT OF INTERNATIONAL FUNDS FOR AGRICULTURAL DEVELOPMENT-VALUE CHAIN DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMME ON WOMEN EMPOWERMENT IN BENUE AND NIGER STATE, NIGERIA
records.venue: International Journal of Financial Research and Business Development
records.abstract: The research was aimed at examining the effects of international funds for agricultural development -value chain development programme on women empowerment in Benue and Niger states, Nigeria. Multi-stage sampling technique was used for the study. First stage was purposively selection of Benue and Niger states in North central. At the second stage, women (producers, processors and marketers of rice) beneficiaries in the programme was purposively selected from three (3) LGAs from each of the state making a total of 6 LGAs, The third and fourth stage involved a purposive selection of LGAs and communities in each State respectively. In all, a total of 330 respondents were selected from the LGA as the sample size for the study. The results showed that the mean age of the respondents in the study area was 49 years in Benue and 47 years in Niger state while the average family size was 7 and 9 person in Benue and Niger states respectively, and 79% and 89% were married in Benue and Niger staes respectively, with almost 33% in Quranic education in Niger and also 33% with primary education in Benue state. 96% and 97% of participating women has access to extension agents in both Niger and Benue states respectively. The result in Table 3 revealed that in Benue State, the majority of the women (98.0%) were able to employ more labourers to work for them in their various enterprises also majority of the women (83.6%) reported they were now able to pay their children’s school fees in Niger state. The distribution according to women perception in VCDP activities in Table 4 shows that in the study areas, the women respondent perceived that IFAD-VCDP was a good project. Factors influencing participation in income-generating activities within the Value Chain Development Programme (VCDP) include socio-economic characteristics, access to inputs and credit, and extension services. This study has also identified and analyzed the various factors influencing women's participation in rice value chain of production, processing and marketing activities under the IFAD Value Chain Development Programme (VCDP). The study recommends that financial institutions and lending agencies should work out modalities for easy access to credit facilities to small holder farmers especially women to expand their agri-business in the study area.

records.title: Sistem Pendukung Keputusan Penerima Dispensasi UKT(Uang Kuliah Tunggal) Di Fakultas Matematika Dan Ilmu Pengetahuan Alam Universitas Sebelas Maret Surakarta dengan AHP ( Analytical Hierarchy Process )
records.abstract: Research Report entitled "Decision Support System for Determining Recipients of UKT Dispensation (Single Tuition Fee) at the Faculty of Mathematics and Natural Sciences UNS with the AHP Method" aims to facilitate the Leaders who will provide UKT relief Dispensation for students who apply for UKT relief Dispensation for applications paid each semester. The many criteria that affect the weight of the score determining the recipient of UKT relief dispensation make it difficult to calculate the amount of weight that has been submitted and the accuracy in determining the weight of the score for each criterion cannot be ascertained, so the Decision Support System with the AHP method is the right method to overcome the problem of determining recipients of UKT dispensation with many supporting criteria submitted. These criteria include UKT Costs, Parental Income, Working Parents, Completeness of Parents, Number of Family Dependents, Number of children in the family, Child No., Status of Siblings applying and education, Ownership status, Electricity Costs/month and Number of Vehicles owned

records.title: The Impact of Women’s Education on the Second Childbirth Interval: Evidence from the 2018 China Migrants Dynamic Survey
records.abstract: Within the significant global fertility rate decline, China’s negative population growth is particularly remarkable. Over 40 years, China has experienced two notable socioeconomic trends: longer birth intervals among women and improved educational levels. Investigating the relationship between these factors will enhance understanding of China’s current challenges and provide essential insights for global population governance. This study aimed to explore the effect and mechanism of women’s education level on the birth interval between first and second childbirths using a Cox regression model and data from the 2018 China Migrants Dynamic Survey. The results showed that: (1) Higher education levels significantly extended the interval before having a second child and reduced the probability of having a second child by 28.5%, while women with residential area-related above-average years of education also significantly delayed having a second child, reducing their likelihood by 20.5%. (2) The income substitution effect significantly moderated the influence of women’s education on the second childbirth interval, with higher income amplifying the impact of education, which further reduced the likelihood of women with higher education or residential areas with above-average years of schooling having a second child, thus extending the interval between births. And (3) The child penalty effect significantly moderated the influence of women’s education on the interval between childbirths. Increased work commitment and more severe penalties for childbearing enhanced the impact of women’s education on the birth interval, reducing the likelihood of having a second child for highly educated women and further prolonging the interval between births.

records.title: A cost analysis comparing seasonal malaria chemoprevention with and without Vitamin A supplementation among under-5 children in Nigeria
records.abstract: BACKGROUND: Child mortality in Nigeria, significantly affected by malaria and malnutrition, remains a public health concern in the country. Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention (SMC) and Vitamin A supplementation (VAS) are effective interventions that can be delivered through integrated health campaigns to reduce this mortality. This study assesses the cost implications of integrating these two interventions among under-5 children in Northeast Nigeria. METHODS: A cost analysis compared standalone SMC (Cycle 1 in July 2021) with SMC-VAS integrated campaign (Cycle 4 in October 2023) in two Local Government Areas (LGAs) in Bauchi State. The number of children reached by the SMC-only campaign was 168,820 and for the SMC + Vit A campaign, the number was 170,681. Data collection utilized a mixed-methods approach, drawing from primary and secondary sources, including programmatic, financial, and coverage records. Costs were categorized into distribution, Sulphadoxine-Pyrimethamine plus Amodaiquine (SPAQ) for SMC, Vitamin A, training, supplies, meetings, labor, supervision, and social mobilization costs. Sensitivity analyses evaluated the effect of a 10% fluctuation in the costs of distribution, labor, SPAQ, and supplies on the cost per child. RESULTS: The total cost for the SMC standalone campaign was US$158,934, and the SMC-VAS integration was US$186,426. Distribution and drug costs were the largest contributors in the integrated and SMC-only campaign. The SMC-only cost per child was $0.94 and $1.18 when eligible children received both SMC and VAS. The integration of VAS into the SMC campaign cycle incurred an additional US$27,492 over Cycle 1 cost (US$186,426 - US$158,934). Fluctuations in distribution costs were the most influential component of the cost per child. CONCLUSION: Integrating VAS with SMC campaigns increases the cost by US$0.24 per child, a modest increment considering the potential health benefits. The results support the feasibility of this integration, in terms of cost, to combat child mortality from malaria and malnutrition in Nigeria. Further research is recommended to explore the cost-effectiveness of this integrated distribution model.

records.title: Who benefits the most? Direct and indirect effects of a free cesarean section policy in Benin
records.abstract: This paper evaluates the causal effect of the access to Benin's free cesarean section policy on females and their children. I use a large sample of Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) for West African countries and analyze how the exemption of the cesarean section user fees for females in Benin directly impacts maternal and infant mortality, family size decisions, and labor market participation. I use a Difference in Differences approach and find that having access to the free cesarean section policy significantly reduces the number of stillbirths and infant mortality by 0.0855 (a 18.79 percentage change). Second, for the surviving children, I find that access to the free cesarean section increases the likelihood of maternal mortality by 0.00465 (a 5.21 percentage change). The policy is effective at reducing infant mortality and saving the newborn. However, it harms the mother's health which translates to lower fertility after the first birth and decreased maternal labor supply post-birth.

records.title: Fertility Choices with Career Risk
records.abstract: Couples decide whether to have children before knowing the persistent career loss generated by parenthood. After the loss is realized, household resources are renegotiated and individual market earnings partly determine outside options. This limited-commitment friction places a disproportionate share of female earnings risk on the wife even when expected household resources are unchanged. We embed this mechanism in a generalized-Nash fertility bargain. The model has a unique positive agreement whenever both spouses have positive marginal gains at zero fertility. A larger expected child penalty and greater career-loss risk reduce agreed fertility. A higher loading of own earnings into outside options reduces fertility precisely when the wife's participation margin dominates the husband's corresponding gain. Insurance against the unexpected component of the career loss raises fertility without subsidizing its mean, whereas a conventional per-child transfer operates only through expected cost. A full-commitment benchmark isolates the risk-sharing distortion. In an illustrative discrete-parity exercise, rising career risk lowers desired family size from three children to two and then one, while partial earnings-loss insurance can restore the three-child outcome. These results identify a policy margin that is not available in a deterministic participation-constraint model: insurance against the distribution of the child penalty.

records.title: Parental leave, family, and firms
records.abstract: We investigate the effects of maternity and paternity leave on families and firms. Drawing on rich administrative data linking generations in Brazil and leveraging a policy reform that expanded parental leave, we evaluate the impacts on parents, their spouses, and children, as well as the broader consequences for firms. Our analysis spans labour market outcomes, fertility, health, and education, offering new evidence on the multifaceted effects of parental leave in a developing country context. We find that mothers eligible for extended leave experience a 6.33 p.p. increase in post-birth employment and a 56.63% rise in earnings, with no significant labour effects for fathers. Regarding fertility decisions, paternity leave accelerates subsequent births among fathers and their partners. Female spouses of treated fathers face a sharper, though temporary, child penalty that fades within two years. Despite the additional time spent with children, we find no evidence of mental health improvements for either parents or spouses. For children, the policy boosts early education enrolment by 11.57 p.p. and improves short-term health during the first 12 months of life. On the firm side, we find sharp contrasts between large and small employers. Large firms experience a modest decline in the share of female workers but an increase in women's representation among top earners, driven primarily by childless women, suggesting a reallocation of career opportunities. Small firms, by contrast, face steep drops in female employment and earnings, reflecting their limited capacity to absorb the costs of extended leave. We further show that firms receiving fiscal compensation to offset the cost of the policy- through tax deductions-maintain or improve female employment, earnings shares, and representation in top positions. Those actively claiming these deductions not only avoid negative impacts but even show net gains for female participation and career advancement.

records.title: Direct and Indirect Effects of Free Cesarean Section Access on Maternal and Infant Outcomes
SOCIO-ECONOMIC FACTORS INFLUENCING PRIMARY SCHOOL DROPOUT AMONG HOUSEHOLDS IN KITUI EAST SUB-COUNTY, KENYA
records.venue: American International Journal of Social Science Research
records.abstract: Despite national reforms like Free Primary Education and the push for universal transition to secondary school, school dropout remains widespread in Kitui East Sub-County. This study examines the socio-economic factors associated with school retention, focusing on parental financial status, education, and involvement. A mixed-methods design was adopted, drawing a sample of 377 households from a population of 17,497 through cluster, random, and purposive sampling. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Chi-square tests, and logistic regression, while qualitative data were thematically analyzed. The results show that 48.7% of households report being unable to afford schooling, which is associated with three times the odds of dropout (OR = 3.20, 95% CI: 1.54–6.62). Financial constraints further increase the risk of dropout (OR = 2.44, 95% CI: 1.20–4.98). Higher parental education is protective, with diploma (OR = 0.34, 95% CI: 0.14–0.84) and degree holders (OR = 0.24, 95% CI: 0.09–0.66) less likely to report dropout. Literacy practices such as reading educational materials (OR = 0.41, 95% CI: 0.19–0.87) and parental involvement through school visits (OR = 0.31, 95% CI: 0.13–0.73) significantly reduce risk. A larger family size is associated with a higher likelihood of dropout (OR = 2.04, 95% CI: 1.08–3.86). Thematic findings reinforce these quantitative results, linking irregular income, high schooling costs, and limited literacy practices to decisions to withdraw children from school. The study indicates that household income security, parental literacy, and active engagement in education are the key household-level factors associated with pupil retention in a rural Kenyan sub-county.

records.title: Peer Review Report For: A demographic dividend of the FP2020 Initiative and the SDG reproductive health target: Case studies of India and Nigeria [version 1; peer review: 3 approved]
records.abstract: Background: The demographic dividend, defined as the economic growth potential resulting from favorable shifts in population age structure following rapid fertility decline, has been widely employed to advocate improving access to family planning. The current framework focuses on the long-term potential, while the short-term benefits may also help persuade policy makers to invest in family planning. Methods: We estimate the short- and medium-term economic benefits from two major family planning goals: the Family Planning 2020 (FP2020)’s goal of adding 120 million modern contraceptive users by 2020; Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) 3.7 of ensuring universal access to family planning by 2030. We apply the cohort component method to World Population Prospects and National Transfer Accounts data. India and Nigeria, respectively the most populous Asian and African country under the FP2020 initiative, are used as case studies. Results: Meeting the FP2020 target implies that on average, the number of children that need to be supported by every 100 working-age people would decrease by 8 persons in India and 11 persons in Nigeria in 2020; the associated reduction remains at 8 persons in India, but increases to 14 persons in Nigeria by 2030 under the SDG 3.7. In India meeting the FP2020 target would yield a saving of US$18.2 billion (PPP) in consumption expenditures for children and youth in the year 2020 alone, and that increased to US$89.7 billion by 2030. In Nigeria the consumption saved would be US$2.5 billion in 2020 and $12.9 billion by 2030. Conclusions: The tremendous economic benefits from meeting the FP2020 and SDG family planning targets demonstrate the cost-effectiveness of investment in promoting access to contraceptive methods. The gap already apparent between the observed and targeted trajectories indicates tremendous missing opportunities. Accelerated progress is needed to achieve the FP2020 and SDG goals and so reap the demographic dividend.
